subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 68-year-old man with a history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes presents for evaluation of intermittent palpitations that began several weeks ago. On examination his pulse is noted to be irregularly irregular with a rate of 96/min. An ECG shows an irregular baseline with no discrete P waves, narrow QRS complexes (<120 msec), and randomly variable intervals between QRS complexes.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_correct: Atrial fibrillation produces an irregularly irregular rate and rhythm with no discrete P waves, exactly as described. It is a supraventricular (narrow-complex) arrhythmia because the ventricles are activated through the normal conduction system. Arrhythmogenic activity usually originates from automatic foci near the pulmonary vein ostia in the left atrium, and common risk factors include hypertension, CAD, advanced age, and atrial dilation — all reflected in this patient's history.

explanation_incorrect.A: Atrial flutter produces rapid, identical, consecutive atrial depolarization waves with a sawtooth appearance and a regular ventricular response (equal RR intervals), not an irregularly irregular rhythm lacking P waves.
explanation_incorrect.C: Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregularly irregular but is distinguished by at least 3 distinct P wave morphologies from multiple ectopic atrial foci; this tracing has no discrete P waves at all.
explanation_incorrect.D: Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia is a regular narrow-complex tachycardia, most often due to a reentrant tract in the AV node, presenting with sudden-onset palpitations, lightheadedness, and diaphoresis.
explanation_incorrect.E: First-degree AV block shows a uniformly prolonged PR interval (>200 msec) with every P wave followed by a QRS complex; the rhythm remains regular and P waves are present.

educationalObjective: Recognize atrial fibrillation as an irregularly irregular supraventricular rhythm with no discrete P waves, arising from automatic foci near the pulmonary vein ostia of the left atrium.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 74-year-old woman with chronic atrial fibrillation who has been inconsistent with anticoagulation is brought to the emergency department after the sudden onset of right arm weakness and slurred speech. Head CT confirms an ischemic stroke. Her cardiologist explains that the arrhythmia causes blood stasis within a cardiac chamber, predisposing to clot formation and embolization.
question: In patients with atrial fibrillation, which of the following cardiac sites is the most common location of thrombus formation giving rise to embolic events?
explanation_correct: Atrial fibrillation may predispose to thromboembolic events, particularly stroke, because of left atrial blood stasis. The left atrial appendage is the most common site of thrombus formation in atrial fibrillation. This is why anticoagulation is central to long-term management, alongside rate and rhythm control.

explanation_incorrect.A: The right atrial appendage is not the described site; the thromboembolic risk of atrial fibrillation stems from stasis in the left atrium, not the right.
explanation_incorrect.B: Mural thrombus in the left ventricle is associated with infarcted or dyskinetic ventricular wall (eg, true ventricular aneurysm), not with atrial fibrillation stasis.
explanation_incorrect.C: The pulmonary vein ostia in the left atrium are where the arrhythmogenic automatic foci of atrial fibrillation originate — they are the source of the rhythm, not the most common thrombus location.
explanation_incorrect.E: The interatrial septum is not a site of thrombus formation in atrial fibrillation; stasis preferentially affects the left atrial appendage.

educationalObjective: The left atrial appendage is the most common site of thrombus formation in atrial fibrillation and the source of embolic strokes.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 70-year-old man with a 45-pack-year smoking history and severe COPD is admitted with worsening dyspnea and a productive cough. His heart rate is 118/min and irregularly irregular. ECG shows an irregularly irregular rhythm with at least three morphologically distinct P waves, variable PR intervals, and narrow QRS complexes.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_correct: Multifocal atrial tachycardia is an irregularly irregular rhythm with at least 3 distinct P wave morphologies, due to multiple ectopic foci firing within the atria. It is classically associated with underlying pulmonary disease (COPD), pneumonia, and heart failure — this patient's COPD exacerbation is the classic setting.

explanation_incorrect.B: Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular but has no discrete P waves; the presence of multiple distinct P wave morphologies points instead to multifocal atrial tachycardia.
explanation_incorrect.C: Atrial flutter shows rapid, identical, consecutive atrial waves producing a sawtooth pattern with a regular ventricular rhythm, not ≥3 different P wave morphologies.
explanation_incorrect.D: Premature atrial contractions are isolated extra beats from ectopic atrial foci with a narrow QRS and a preceding P wave, not a sustained irregularly irregular tachycardia with multiple P wave morphologies.
explanation_incorrect.E: Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia is typically regular and arises from a reentrant tract, most commonly in the AV node; it presents with sudden palpitations, lightheadedness, and diaphoresis.

educationalObjective: Multifocal atrial tachycardia is an irregularly irregular rhythm with ≥3 distinct P wave morphologies and is associated with COPD, pneumonia, and heart failure.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 66-year-old woman is found on routine ECG to have a regular heart rate of 75/min. The tracing shows rapid succession of identical, consecutive atrial depolarization waves producing a characteristic sawtooth appearance, with every fourth atrial wave followed by a narrow QRS complex.
question: Which of the following mechanisms best explains the atrial depolarizations seen in this patient?

options.text: Automatic foci near the pulmonary vein ostia in the left atrium
Reentrant tract within the AV node
Reentry circuit around the tricuspid annulus
Multiple ectopic foci within the atria
Accessory pathway (bundle of Kent) bypassing the AV node

explanation_correct: The sawtooth pattern of rapid, identical, consecutive atrial depolarization waves is characteristic of atrial flutter, in which arrhythmogenic activity usually originates from a reentry circuit around the tricuspid annulus. Atrial flutter is managed like atrial fibrillation, with the option of catheter ablation of the region between the tricuspid annulus and the inferior vena cava, which interrupts the circuit.

explanation_incorrect.A: Automatic foci near the pulmonary vein ostia in the left atrium drive atrial fibrillation, which produces irregular fibrillatory activity without discrete P waves or a sawtooth pattern.
explanation_incorrect.B: A reentrant tract involving the AV node explains paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia, not the atrial circuit responsible for flutter waves.
explanation_incorrect.D: Multiple ectopic atrial foci cause multifocal atrial tachycardia, in which P waves have at least 3 distinct morphologies; flutter waves are rapid and identical to one another.
explanation_incorrect.E: The bundle of Kent bypasses the AV node in Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, producing a delta wave, widened QRS, and shortened PR interval — not atrial sawtooth waves.

educationalObjective: Atrial flutter is caused by a reentry circuit around the tricuspid annulus, producing rapid identical atrial waves with a sawtooth appearance.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 24-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset palpitations, lightheadedness, and diaphoresis. Her heart rate is 185/min and regular, and blood pressure is 108/70 mm Hg. ECG demonstrates a regular, narrow-complex (QRS 90 msec) tachycardia without discernible P waves. Vagal maneuvers performed at the bedside fail to terminate the episode.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy to terminate this patient's arrhythmia?
explanation_correct: This is paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia, most often due to a reentrant tract between atrium and ventricle, most commonly in the AV node. Episodes present with sudden-onset palpitations, lightheadedness, and diaphoresis and are terminated by slowing AV nodal conduction — first with vagal maneuvers, then with adenosine. Definitive treatment, if episodes recur, is catheter ablation.

explanation_incorrect.A: Amiodarone is a class III antiarrhythmic used for ventricular arrhythmias and rhythm control in atrial fibrillation; it is not the first-line agent to terminate AV nodal reentrant tachycardia.
explanation_incorrect.B: Atropine is an antimuscarinic that increases SA and AV nodal conduction and heart rate; it would worsen a reentrant tachycardia and is used for symptomatic bradycardia.
explanation_incorrect.C: Lidocaine is a class IB agent acting on ventricular (ischemic or depolarized) tissue and is ineffective for arrhythmias whose circuit depends on the AV node.
explanation_incorrect.D: Isoproterenol is a β-adrenergic agonist that accelerates AV nodal conduction and automaticity, which would promote rather than terminate the reentry circuit.

educationalObjective: PSVT is a reentrant tachycardia, most commonly at the AV node, terminated by vagal maneuvers and adenosine; definitive treatment is catheter ablation.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 19-year-old man presents with sudden palpitations and presyncope; he has had similar self-limited episodes since adolescence. A previously obtained baseline ECG shows a shortened PR interval, a widened QRS complex, and a slurred initial upstroke of the QRS (delta wave). He is currently in a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 200/min with stable vital signs.
question: Which of the following medications is the most appropriate treatment for this patient's current arrhythmia?
explanation_correct: This patient has Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, the most common type of ventricular preexcitation syndrome. An abnormal fast accessory pathway from atria to ventricle (the bundle of Kent) bypasses the rate-slowing AV node, causing ventricles to partially depolarize earlier — producing the delta wave, widened QRS, and shortened PR interval — and may create a reentry circuit causing supraventricular tachycardia. Treatment of the tachycardia is with procainamide or ibutilide.

explanation_incorrect.A: Adenosine is an AV nodal–blocking drug, which is specifically avoided in Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome; agents that slow the AV node are contraindicated here.
explanation_incorrect.C: Verapamil is a calcium channel blocker that slows AV nodal conduction, an approach avoided in WPW because of the accessory pathway.
explanation_incorrect.D: Metoprolol is a β-blocker that slows AV nodal conduction; β-blockers are on the list of AV nodal–blocking drugs to avoid in WPW.
explanation_incorrect.E: Digoxin slows AV nodal conduction and is used for rate control in atrial fibrillation, but AV nodal–blocking strategies are avoided in WPW.

educationalObjective: In Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, treat reentry tachycardias with procainamide or ibutilide and avoid AV nodal–blocking drugs (adenosine, calcium channel blockers, β-blockers).
